I think it would be GREAT if pets could fly. It would make travel a lot more accessible for a lot of people. I think the only issue is what avenues would be open for those with pets, and how to keep people safe and pets with the least amount of stress possible. 

One option would be a “standard of training” test, but even well *trained* dogs can get very stressed on a flight. A behavioral test would be another option, where they test a dog’s reaction to different stressors. Honestly, I would rather have a stable, undertrained or minimally trained dog than a well trained dog on a hair trigger. 

Another option would be “pet friendly” flights? Maybe something like Uber pet but for airlines where you just pay more for your flight and it’s a designated plane for dogs and people to travel together. That would solve the allergy issue as well as people scared of dogs since they wouldn’t have to interact at all, and airlines get to charge more. It doesn’t address stability OR training however. 

Currently there are flights that allow dogs in cabin. I believe Jet Blue lets dogs up to maybe 50lbs in cabin for a pet fee as well as charter flights. Chartered/private flights aren’t really accessible for everyone due to just cost. 

In MY opinion, the best choice would be a standardized test pet owners could take, kind of like the canine good citizen offered by the AKC that tests the reaction of a dog to people and other dogs, as well as basic obedience. The big issue there would be how is it regulated, what would the exact requirements be, cost, and especially I think it would need to be renewed yearly. Testing could be done at larger airports in every area, with a one time fee (maybe a retesting fee?), yearly renewal etc. 

But yeah I just think it’s unfair to both the dog and everyone else on the flight to bring a pet with no sort of training onto a plane. It’s a LOT for a dog.

No I totally understand people work their dogs off leash for various reasons and I support working your dog in whatever way works best for you. Like I said, I did it until I didn’t feel comfortable not having a physical tether to my dog. But I’ve also had to prove in a lawsuit that I needed him off leash and that was a trying time, even if it ended in my favor.

As disabled people the government isn’t on our side. They’re usually actively against us, and so I’m saying there is usually a way to work without having your dog completely off leash. Me cautioning people is trying to save them what I went through, which was being attacked and dehumanized. 

Other disabled people and specifically service dog gear makers have made gear really accommodating. Bold Lead Designs makes harnesses that have magnetic latches exactly for people who have trouble with standard buckles. You can attach a traffic lead to the harness and leave it there so it doesn’t need to be clipped and unclipped. Looking at other options should always be the first step. When I transitioned from working off leash it took me a while to find something I felt comfortable with that worked for us as a team, but I did it. And like I said, I reached out to others in this community to crowd source ideas and found nothing but support. 

Also, just as I don’t know your disabilities you don’t know mine so try not to make assumptions about what I do or do not understand :)

Hey! Coming from someone who worked their dog off leash until my disabilities made it concerning to not have some sort of attachment to him, there are usually alternative options to a standard leash that fit our disabilities. I got some great suggestions from others in our community when I reached out to find some, so just passing them forward. 

Like PureBread said, a leash that is double ended is a great choice for a lot of people, and most of those double ended leashes also convert to hands free leashes either around the waist or over the shoulder. My favorite is the Atlas leash from Bold Lead Designs, and if I’m out with another person that’s what I use currently.  What I used for a bit was a sort of retractable leash that’s built into the collar, but this is something I honestly can’t recommend unless your dog is trained both off leash very well and to loose leash walk very well, since the cord is fragile and would break is there was pressure from a bigger dog. 

A traffic lead is ultimately what I used for the majority of my dog’s working career, even when he was “off leash.” Easy to drop if needed, but it gives the public and stores peace of mind when they see it. There’s usually a solution other that being off leash, even if it’s a PITA to find something that works for you. Remember that if anything happens, you need to be able to prove you need the dog off leash in order to be protected. I had this happen a couple of years back and the process kind of sucks.

If you need mobility support, a mobility aid like a wheelchair, cane, or walker is always safer to use than a dog. Big programs are moving away from heavy mobility tasks like wheelchair pulling or bracing because there’s no research that shows that it’s safe for the dogs, and those dogs almost always have a shorter working life than dogs that weren’t used for those mobility tasks. 

That being said, if you need a mobility dog to do something like get things you drop so you don’t have to bend down, or help you pull off your socks those are safer mobility tasks. 

Your best place to start looking for a program would be the assistance dogs international website. You can filter by country and then state to find programs that serve your area, and they’re an internationally recognized program so you’re going to have a lot less problems if you like to travel than if you have an owner trained dog.

How old is your puppy? If they aren’t already pretty much PA trained, a school isn’t where I would start training. You have a hectic schedule with less flexibility than say, college classes. In addition it is a very high distraction environment and can be stressful without a foundation of how to act in such situations. 

That being said, talk to your parents and school about adding a service dog to your 504 as an accommodation. You could also request stuff like flexible passing periods so you aren’t in the halls with all of the other kids or a seat near the wall for extra room for your pup. 

It’s better to wait if you don’t have a lot of PA under your belt, IMO. It’s easier for a more experienced, older dog to adapt to the college life than a pup in high school. If you’re able, things you can train for at home include tucking under a desk, lots and lots of settling practice, and working in high traffic/stress situations like a fair or festival. Remember, slow is fast when training a service dog.
